tutorial.callThought: So much for a quiet morning. I’d better head into the forge.
tutorial.callMessage: All right, Dad, I’m coming… So much for a quiet morning. I’d better head into the forge.
tutorial.chooseEnter: Now choose the house icon to enter the forge.
tutorial.fatherMessage: Morning, son. The ore bin’s nearly empty again. Bring me four lumps of iron ore and four of coal from the market, will you?
tutorial.fatherWorkReply: What are you worried about? We finally have enough work to keep us busy all day, and we’ve paid off our debts. I’d take a busy forge over an empty one.
tutorial.leaveForIron: I’ll bring everything back. Then we can start.
tutorial.acceptErrand: More ore already? We’ve been going through so many supplies these past few months.
tutorial.lockedPlace: This location is not available yet.
tutorial.firstBlade: You’ve done well with all the chores I’ve given you. Tomorrow’s your birthday—you’ll be counted a grown man then. I think it’s time you made a dagger of your own. I’ll help you through the first one.
tutorial.firstBladeReply: A dagger? You mean I’ll make the whole thing myself?
tutorial.firstBladeThought: My first real weapon. I’ve watched Dad make so many, wondering when he’d let me try. I can already picture it in my hand. I’d better not keep him waiting.
tutorial.fittingsRequest: The whole thing. Pick up a plain wooden guard, handle and pommel while you’re there. Nothing fancy for the first one. Get the supplies home, and we’ll see what you can do.

tavern.greeting: There you are, lad. Your usual place is free, if you’re after a bite. Or did you come about the notice I put up at the market?

answer.bandits: Some thieves took a handful of my coin on the road. I could use a little work to make it back.
answer.father: Dad’s finally letting me make a dagger. I was fetching supplies when I ran into trouble on the road. Is that work on your notice still going?
answer.work: I saw your notice at the market, Oswin. Do you still need a hand?

reply.bandits: Road thieves again? I am sorry, lad. The woodpile needs splitting, and there are dishes in the kitchen. Do either job well and I will pay you.
reply.father: Your first blade, is it? About time he let you have a go. There’s work here if you want it—wood for the hearth or dishes in the kitchen. I’ll pay when it’s done.
reply.work: I do. The firewood needs splitting and the kitchen’s got a stack of dishes. Take your pick, and I’ll pay you when the job’s finished.

marketNotice.title: A notice by the stalls
marketNotice.reflection: I’ve walked these stalls since I was small. Today, everyone seems a little quieter. Another empty stall, another argument over prices… and now thieves on the road. I wonder how long things can carry on like this.
marketNotice.money: Father’s waiting for the materials, and I’m short of coin now. I’ll need to earn a little before I can buy everything. There’s a notice pinned beside the stalls. Perhaps someone needs a hand.
marketNotice.notice:
HELP WANTED AT THE INN
A spare pair of hands needed for washing dishes or splitting firewood. Coin paid for the work. Ask the innkeeper.

The inn isn’t far. I could see what he needs.
marketNotice.moneyThought: Father’s waiting for the materials. I’ll need to make up the missing coin somehow.

workshop.title: Father’s workshop
workshop.materialsOnly: Only materials can be stored here.
workshop.capacity: My bag cannot hold any more weight.
workshop.coalNeeded: I need coal in my bag, and room in the fire.
workshop.sameOre: A charge needs four pieces of the same ore.
workshop.chargeNeeded: Load four ore and one coal, then light the forge.
workshop.mouldBusy: The metal must be molten and the mould empty.
workshop.ironOnly: This blank does not match my active design.
workshop.workingHeat: The metal is outside its working range.
workshop.quenchHeat: The metal is outside its quenching range.
workshop.hammerNeeded: Equip the crude hammer before working the blade.
workshop.allCells: Each cell needs at least one blow.
workshop.partsNeeded: I need the next fitting in my bag: wooden guard, handle, then pommel.
workshop.source: Choose a source for each piece. Mixed ore charges are not allowed.
workshop.hammerHelp: I’ll hold to raise my hammer, then release to strike a region. Each region rises toward 100%, then falls if I keep working it. At zero from overworking, the blade is ruined. I’ll reheat it when it grows cold.
workshop.quenchHelp: I’ll heat the shaped metal into its quenching range, then hold it in water or oil. The score rises toward 100%, then falls; going too far ruins the blade. Water cools it faster than oil.
workshop.assemblyHelp: Enter the frame to capture the mouse, then move left and right to align the fitting. Click either mouse button to drop it. Each fitting starts up to 20 px off-centre and moves within 30 px of the dagger’s centre. On touchscreens, drag and release inside the frame. Esc releases the mouse.
workshop.grindHelp: I’ll bring the blade against the upright wheel and move it across. Lifting or lowering it changes how the edge meets the stone. I’ll watch the sparks, then draw it away before turning it over.
workshop.noBlade: Heat an iron ingot from the rack to begin a dagger.
workshop.nextQuench: The blade is shaped. Reheat it, then choose water or oil.
workshop.nextAssembly: The blade is quenched. Fit its guard, handle and pommel at the workbench.
workshop.nextGrind: The fittings are in place. Take the dagger to the grinding wheel.
workshop.temperatureHelp: Bellows sustain the heat; coal burns over time. Ore is reduced before the metal melts. Heat and cooling continue while I work.
workshop.overheating: Too hot to hammer. Let it cool off the coals.
workshop.recoverQuench: Reheat to try the quench again
workshop.storageHelp: Move materials manually. Storage has no weight limit; my bag holds 30 kg.
workshop.returnLocked: I should bring back four iron ore, four coal, a wooden guard, a wooden handle and a wooden pommel before heading home.
workshop.referenceIntro: Father’s notes are here beside the designs. I can look over the temperatures and the order of the work.

reference.iron: Iron ore contains iron oxides. First reduce the ore with carbon in the hot charge; ore is not simply melted straight into iron. Reduction begins at 1,000°C in this workshop. Reduced iron melts at the game’s reference temperature of 1,538°C. Actual melting behaviour varies with carbon and impurities.
reference.copper: Copper melts at 1,085°C. For an equal-volume stock unit, use 6 sorted copper ore and 1 reducing coal, plus furnace fuel. Copper is denser but softer than iron; it loses its edge sooner. Quenching copper cools it without hardening it.
reference.process: For my first dagger, I need four iron ore and one reducing coal in the crucible, with furnace fuel added separately. My later designs list their own charge and fittings. I’ll let the metal reduce and melt, then wait until both metal and crucible are 100°C above the melting point before pouring. Once the blank has cooled, I can reheat it into its material’s working range and shape every region on both faces. Then I’ll heat it for quenching, cool it carefully in water or oil, fit the guard, handle and pommel, and sharpen whichever edges I designed.

workshop.heatDamage: Heat penalty: −{quality} points. Holding a blade at working heat gradually recovers this penalty.
workshop.thermalHelp: The forge gradually loses heat toward room temperature. Each bellows press adds a short boost; hotter fires gain less. Coal sustains combustion, and water helps the forge cool.
workshop.noSupplies: I need four matching ore pieces, reducing coal and fuel, or an iron ingot before I can begin. I can collect supplies from the storehouse or buy them at the market. Fuel coal needs to be in my bag. For my first dagger, I also need to bring home the wooden guard, handle and pommel Father asked for.
workshop.startFirst: Start blacksmithing at the forge first.
workshop.stopForStorage: End blacksmithing before opening the storehouse.
workshop.bellowsRecovering: Let the bellows refill for a moment.
workshop.pouringHelp: Hold the crucible and lift it to pour. Higher pours flow faster; lifting too high spills metal. Release to lower it and pause. Resume while the mould is still liquid. Aim to fill at least 95% before the metal hardens. A steady pour takes about 5–6 seconds.
workshop.dragCrucible: Hold and lift crucible to pour. Keyboard: hold Space and use Up or Down; release Space to lower.
workshop.castingFailed: The casting is ruined. Discard it at the mould. Reheat any crucible leftovers to melting point before discarding them.
workshop.castingFinished: The ingot is cooling in the mould. Any crucible leftovers must be reheated and discarded before a fresh charge.
workshop.finishPourFirst: Finish the current pour before working another station.
workshop.residueCold: Reheat the remaining metal until it is fully molten before discarding it.
workshop.residueHelp: This metal cannot be used for another ingot. Reheat it until fully molten, then discard it before loading a fresh charge.
workshop.assemblyAim: Enter to capture the mouse. Move left/right, then left- or right-click to drop. Touch: drag and release inside. Keyboard: arrows to aim, Enter or Space to drop. Esc releases capture.

forgeLesson.title: At Father’s forge
ore: Your first proper blade, then. Start with four pieces of the same ore in the crucible. Choose them from your bag or the storehouse; keep the metals separate.
I do know which end of the crucible is open, Dad. I’ve been watching you since I could see over the bench.
Still, I’m glad he’s staying nearby. Watching his hands was rather easier than trusting my own.
reducer: Now one piece of coal into the charge as the reducing agent. Heating ore alone is not enough: the carbon helps free the metal from its oxygen. This coal belongs in the crucible; the fire needs its own fuel.
One for the metal, more for the fire. Yes, I remember. I was listening, even when I looked as though I wasn’t.
fuel: Feed some coal to the forge from your bag. A piece will burn for a good while, so there’s no need to heap it in. If your fuel is in storage, end blacksmithing and fetch it first.
He has that look again—the one that means he knows exactly how much coal I was about to waste. One piece first, then.
crucible: The charge and fuel are ready. Put the crucible onto the forge with the heat-crucible action. We’ll bring the fire up together.
bellows: Work the bellows in steady presses. Each stroke gives a short burst of heat, and a hotter fire gains less from it. The heat is always escaping, so watch it rather than pumping without looking.
Steady hands, watch the colour, don’t fight the fire. I might have heard that once or twice in this house.
melting: The metal is melting. Iron’s melting point is about 1,538 degrees, but do not lift it at the first sign of liquid. Wait for a fully molten charge, with both the metal and crucible at least 100 degrees hotter—about 1,638 for iron. We need that stored heat for carrying and pouring.
I had been about to lift it. Best give it a little longer, as though that was my plan all along.
pour: The charge is fully liquid, and both it and the crucible have at least a hundred degrees in reserve above melting. Lift it now and carry it to the mould. Hold and raise it to pour; a moderate height takes five or six seconds. Keep the casting liquid and get at least ninety-five percent into the mould. Watch both temperatures as you work.
I’ve seen you do this without spilling a drop. You could have made it look a little harder, for my sake.
ruined: This casting won’t do. Click the mould to discard it. Don’t try to hide a cold join beneath more metal. We’ll clear the crucible, prepare another charge, and do it properly.
He hasn’t raised his voice. Somehow that makes me want to get the next one right even more.
residue: There’s metal left in the crucible. Reheat it until fully molten, then give both the metal and crucible a hundred degrees above melting before lifting it to discard. We cannot use the leftovers to top up a casting that has already set.
collect: The ingot has cooled enough to lift out. Take it from the mould; we’ll keep it on the rack beside the forge until you’re ready to work it.
ingot: Now put an iron ingot onto the coal. If it’s in your bag, set it on the rack first and choose it there. Melting gave us stock; the anvil will give it a blade’s shape.
Finally, the part with the hammer. I promise I was paying attention to the rest as well.
heatBlade: Bring the ingot to about 900 degrees, then lift it off the coal before walking to the anvil. It can be worked from 750 to 1,150, but starting at the lowest heat leaves no time to carry it or work. Give yourself that margin.
hammer: There—about 900 degrees. Take the ingot off the forge now, then carry it to the anvil. Hold over a cell to raise the hammer, then release to strike. Work all sixteen areas toward one hundred; further blows overwork them, and reheating cannot undo that.
All sixteen, even blows, and stop before I’m improving it into scrap. You make a very convincing case for a light touch.
His eyes are on the blade rather than my hands now. Perhaps he thinks I can do this after all.
reheat: The blade needs another heat. Bring it back to about 900 degrees before taking it off the coal. That leaves time to walk back and work before it cools below 750. There’s no prize for beating cold iron.
shape: You’ve worked every part. Look over the scores before you finish shaping; untouched and overworked patches will stay with the blade. When you’re satisfied, finish the shape and we’ll quench it.
quenchHeat: Bring the shaped blade to about 850 degrees before taking it off the coal for quenching. The working range is 750 to 900, but leaving at 750 lets it cool too far before it reaches the barrel. If it is too hot, lift it off and let it settle first.
quench: That leaves enough heat for the short walk. Take it off the coal, choose water or oil and hold to quench. Water reaches the sweet spot in about two and a half seconds; oil takes a little over four. Release near one hundred. We can reheat and retry a missed treatment.
I remember the first time you let me near those barrels. You stood rather closer than you are now.
guard: Now to the design bench. Fit the wooden guard first: enter the frame, line it up over the tang, then click. On a touchscreen, drag and lift your finger inside. Keep the fit centred; a tidy blade deserves more than a crooked hilt.
I can almost hear him finding fault with a crooked guard from the other side of the room. Better spare us both the trouble.
handle: The guard is seated. Do the same with the handle, straight down over the tang. Take a moment to line it up, then click to let it fall. The pommel goes on after it.
You know, Dad, it does look remarkably like a dagger now. I’m choosing to take that as encouragement.
grind: Finish at the grinding wheel. Hold the dagger against the upright wheel and move it across. Move up and down to lift or lower the blade; its width shows the tilt. Keep the angle near fifteen degrees. All overlapping areas are worked together. Release before turning it over, and check both sides before finishing.
finished: Thank you, Dad. For staying with me through it, I mean. It helped. But I think I can manage the next one without a voice over my shoulder.
Good. I was hoping to get some work of my own done. Just remember which way round the crucible goes.
I shall carry that lesson with me always. Along with the other twenty you managed to fit into one dagger.
I turn the finished blade in my hand. He trusted me with this. Next time, I want him to see I deserved it.
pommel: The handle is seated. Fit the pommel last, straight over the end of the tang. It holds the grip together and gives the dagger its balance. Centre it as carefully as the other two fittings.
One last piece. I was just beginning to think I could call it finished without you finding something else.

design.intro: I can plan my own weapon here: shape the metal, choose its edges and point, then match it with a grip and fittings.
design.locked: This design is locked while its metal is being worked. Finish or discard the ruined work before changing it.
design.name: Weapon name
design.curveHelp: Drag the three red controls to bend the whole blade. Arrow keys also move a focused control. The tang stays at the origin; X and Y are centimetres. Each stock unit adds three sections and two working faces.
design.recipe: Charge: {ore} {type}, {carbon} reducing coal, plus {fuel} fuel coal. Blank mass: {mass} kg. Fittings must be in my bag.
design.noRecovery: Ruined blades cannot be repaired or recovered. Unused stock becomes forging waste; finished weight follows the actual shape.

issues.invalid: Choose a valid material, point, and fittings.
issues.metalBudget: This shape needs more metal. Add stock or reduce the dimensions.
issues.bendBudget: The combined bend is too large. Bring the curve controls closer to the axis.
issues.folded: The blade folds into itself. Spread out the controls or reduce the bend.
issues.gripCollision: The blade overlaps the grip. Move its curve away from the tang.
issues.weakTransition: A sharp change in section size weakens the weapon. Match neighbouring sections more closely.
issues.thinBlade: This long, thin blade will have lower durability.
issues.softCopper: Copper is dense but soft: lower strength and edge retention than iron. Quenching copper does not harden it.
issues.shortGrip: A longer handle would give this large blade better leverage.
issues.lengthBudget: Each stock unit supports up to 20 cm of metal length. Add stock or shorten the design.
